question: How does silence become part of a theme?
intro: Haydn opens the C major quartet with a bold first-violin gesture and then stops all four players. Listen for how often the music pauses, and for the A♭ in the bass that answers C within the first twenty seconds.

sections.label: Exposition · C major to G major
Recapitulation · the opening returns
sections.mNote: opening gesture returns in C, again over an A♭ bass

cues.title: A gesture, then silence
cues.text: The first violin throws out a turning figure over held low notes, forte; then the score calls for general pauses (G.P.), when all four players stop. Laurie Shulman notes irregular five-bar phrases and dramatic pauses in this movement.
cues.evidence: The Eulenburg score (IMSLP #05812) marks G.P. across all four staves twice within its first dozen bars; Laurie Shulman’s programme note describes the five-measure phrases and pauses. The recording starts at −13.4 dB and falls to −25.8 dB by 0:10, consistent with a pause, but no pause is timed.

cues.title: A♭ beneath the gesture
cues.text: After the pause the gesture returns over an A♭ in the cello, pulling C major towards C minor within seconds. Listen for this flat-side colour: it comes back when the opening returns.
cues.evidence: At 0:15–0:20 the report’s local key reads C minor (r 0.90–0.91) with A♭, E♭ and C as the strongest pitch classes and A♭ in the bass; a boundary falls at 0:14 (novelty 0.86). The score shows an A♭ bass under the restated gesture; the audio match is approximate.

cues.title: The road to G major
cues.text: Listen for the harmony heading towards the dominant. The local key estimate moves through A minor and D major, and by a minute in the quartet has reached G major, where the second group sits. The texture lightens as it arrives.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is A minor at 0:30–0:40, D major at 0:45–0:55 and G major from 1:00 to about 1:30 (r 0.80–0.91); boundaries at 0:44 (0.88) and 1:02 (0.47). Estimates from audio confirm a key region; they do not locate a chord.

cues.title: Tost and the first violin
cues.text: Johann Tost gave his name to the quartets of Opp. 54 and 55. He was second violinist in the Esterházy orchestra from 1783 to 1788, then went to Paris with six new Haydn quartets and two symphonies and arranged for Sieber to publish them.
cues.evidence: Shulman’s note gives Tost’s service and his late-1788 trip to Paris, and says his precise involvement in Opp. 54–55 is less clear; IMSLP lists Tost as dedicatee and Sieber (Paris, 1789) as first publisher: https://imslp.org/wiki/String_Quartets,_Op.54_(Haydn,_Joseph).

cues.title: The development opens loudly
cues.text: The exposition closes quietly in G major. Then a forte statement of the opening gesture over sustained chords begins the development, which turns to the flat side: the key estimate passes through F major and D minor before the music gathers speed.
cues.evidence: A strong boundary falls at 1:32 (novelty 0.99); the local key reads F major from 1:35 and D minor around 1:50. The score shows a piano close of the exposition, endings 1 and 2, and a forte restatement with flat-side harmony; this recording evidently omits the repeat. Bars are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tel Aviv, May 2015
cues.text: This is a live performance by the Danish String Quartet at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art, filmed in May 2015. The audio comes from the museum’s concert video, which was released under a Creative Commons attribution licence.
cues.evidence: The video description (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dGgmFFMFICc) gives venue and month, though it misprints Op. 64 where the title says Op. 54 No. 2; the Commons file page carries the YouTube CC-BY licence template.

cues.title: The opening comes home
cues.text: After the bass has rested on G, the gesture returns in C major and again meets an A♭ bass a few bars later. Compare it with the start: the same shape, but now it closes the argument rather than opening it.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches the opening, 2.5–22.0 s, with 140.0–159.5 s (similarity 0.96, no transposition). The report has G in the bass at 2:15–2:25, then a boundary at 2:30 (0.80) with A♭ in the bass and a C-minor estimate. The first bar of the return is not aligned.

cues.title: The lilting second group, now in C
cues.text: The gentle second-group music, marked p dolce and heard in G major in the exposition, comes back a fourth higher, in C. Listen for the same light writing, now with the home key beneath it.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 62.5–75.0 s with 185.0–197.5 s at a transposition of five semitones upward (G to C; similarity 0.92, weaker than the opening match). The score marks p dolce at the start of the second group (IMSLP #05812, p. 181); bars are not aligned.

cues.title: A loud stretch near the end
cues.text: Near 3:25 the level jumps by about twenty decibels into a long, loud passage with fast repeated notes in the upper strings. It is one of the loudest stretches of the movement and drives towards the final cadence.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 3:26 (1.00): relative level rises from −28.2 dB at 3:20 to −8.4 dB at 3:25, and the loudest windows include 3:25 and 3:40 (attack density 4.4 per second). The score has a loud passage with repeated notes in this region; the exact bar is not aligned.

cues.title: Quiet, then the last chords
cues.text: The loud stretch gives way to a quiet passage, and then the level rises once more for the closing bars. Compare this ending with the opening: the pauses are gone, and the movement stops by arriving, not by breaking off.
cues.evidence: Level falls to −24.4 dB at 3:55 with attack density 1.4 per second, then rises to −11.9 dB at 4:05 with a C-major estimate (r 0.95); the file ends at 4:23. The ending is described from the score’s closing chords; bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: A quiet close, then a loud restart
transitions.how: The exposition ends piano in G major. Instead of settling, Haydn restarts with the first violin’s opening gesture, forte, over sustained low chords whose notes include flats, so G major is left at once for the flat side. The dynamic jump and the harmonic swerve make the development sound like a new beginning rather than a continuation, and the stretch that follows keeps returning to the first idea.
transitions.evidence: A strong boundary falls at 1:32 (0.99) and the key estimate moves from G major to F major and D minor by 1:35–1:50. The score shows a piano close with endings 1 and 2 and a forte restatement with flats after it; this recording does not appear to repeat the exposition, and the bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: The gesture returns over the dominant
transitions.how: The development comes to rest with the bass on G, the dominant, and the opening first-violin gesture then returns in C major. A few bars later the A♭ sonority that coloured the opening appears again. Haydn thus prepares the tonic by a brief halt on the dominant, then restores the first bars with their original harmonic shadow, which makes the recapitulation audibly the same story told again.
transitions.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches the opening (2.5–22.0 s) with 140.0–159.5 s; the report has G in the bass at 2:15–2:25, then a boundary at 2:30 (0.80) with A♭ in the bass and a C-minor estimate. The score shows the gesture restated in C and again over A♭; the first bar of the return is not aligned.

source.locator: IMSLP #05812, I. Vivace, printed pp. 179–187; times follow the boundary at 1:32 and the recurrence analysis at 140 s and are approximate.

timeline.note: First violin throws out the turning gesture over held notes in the other three; general pauses follow.
Development: the gesture again in the first violin over sustained low chords.
Recapitulation: the opening gesture returns in C major.

composer.epithet: A court musician who taught the symphony and quartet to argue with the listener’s expectations.
facts: Choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna; practical instruction from Nicola Porpora
Esterházy household, 1761–1809; active court duties reduced after 1790
Visits in 1791–92 and 1794–95; twelve symphonies for the English public
104 numbered symphonies · string quartets · keyboard sonatas and trios · masses · operas · oratorios
composer.background:
Haydn was born in Rohrau, near the border between Lower Austria and Hungary, in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who sang and played the harp by ear; his mother had worked as a cook. Music began at home. After early schooling in Hainburg, he became a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. The work gave him daily experience of church music and a singer’s understanding of phrases, but little systematic composition teaching. When his voice broke, he lost the position and had to earn his living outside the cathedral.

In the 1750s he taught, accompanied and played whatever engagements he could obtain. Working for the singing teacher and composer Nicola Porpora gave him practical instruction in Italian vocal style. He studied scores and keyboard music, including the sonatas of C. P. E. Bach, whose sudden contrasts offered another model besides the regular phrases of the fashionable galant style. Employment by Count Morzin in the late 1750s brought an orchestra and the first symphonies. In 1760 he married Maria Anna Keller; the marriage was unhappy and childless. His professional stability came from a different household.
